items.summary:
ESMA updates its manual on transparency with new guidance for OTC derivatives and tick-size regime 
  
  15 October 2026 
 

       
               Trading 
           
  
              The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU regulator and supervisor, has updated its  manual on transparency  to provide further guidance on the identification of over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives subject to transparency requirements and to enhance supervisory convergence on the application of the tick-size regime. 
 
      
               The update also clarifies how the identifying reference data for OTC derivatives should be provided for transparency purposes, supporting greater consistency in the data reported to and published through the consolidated tape.   
  The manual finally includes several published    Q&As    on the tick size regime, as well as the addition of recommendations on the application of the tick-size regime, comprising when trading venues and national competent authorities may intervene in specific circumstances.

items.summary:
One year to go for T+1 settlement: the regulatory framework is complete, now let’s make it happen 
  
  16 October 2026 
 

       
               Guidelines and Technical standards 
               Post Trading 
               Press Releases 
           
  
               The European Union (EU) will switch to T+1 settlement on 11 October 2027. Ahead of the transition, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, calls on market participants to finalise technical preparations, assess readiness across their entire ecosystems and begin testing as soon as possible throughout the trading and settlement chain.

The first deadline is for investment firms and their clients to comply with the new requirements on allocations and confirmations from   7 December 2026.

items.title: ESMA finalises the review of guidelines on the delay in disclosure of inside information
items.summary:
ESMA finalises the review of guidelines on the delay in disclosure of inside information 
  
  16 October 2026 
 

       
               Guidelines and Technical standards 
               Market Abuse 
               Market Integrity 
               Simplification and Burden Reduction 
           
  
              The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has updated and streamlined its  Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) guidelines on the delay in the disclosure of inside information , completing the revised regulatory framework. 
 
      
              Under MAR, issuers are required to disclose as soon as possible the inside information concerning them, to ensure that investors are informed and to prevent insider dealing. In specific circumstances, issuers may delay public disclosure to avoid prejudicing their legitimate interests.

items.summary:
ESMA specifies requirements to facilitate safe use of post-trade risk reduction services 
  
  20 October 2026 
 

       
               Guidelines and Technical standards 
               Post Trading 
           
  
              The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has outlined the conditions that providers and users of post-trade risk reduction (PTRR) services need to meet for certain OTC derivative transactions to be exempt from the clearing obligation under EMIR 3. The new rules, published in its latest  final report,  also establish safeguards for the provision of these services and the monitoring of the use of the exemption. 
 
      
               With these new rules in place, the goal is to facilitate the use of PTRR services and ensure that the exemption is used under the conditions laid down in EMIR 3 and does not lead to the misuse of the clearing obligation.

items.title: ESMA proposes simpler EU Taxonomy reporting
items.summary:
ESMA proposes simpler EU Taxonomy reporting 
  
  29 October 2026 
 

       
               Issuer disclosure 
               Sustainable finance 
           
  
              The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has published its  Final Report providing technical advice to the European Commission  on simplifying key performance indicators under the Taxonomy Disclosures Delegated Act. 
 
      
              ESMA recommends narrowing the mandatory operating expenditure (OpEx) KPI to non-capitalised research and development expenditure. It also proposes simpler group Taxonomy reporting, including removing the weighted-average KPI, and targeted measures to make disclosures more proportionate, clearer and easier to use.  
 The Technical Advice was coordinated with the other European Supervisory Authorities, in particular on the voluntary use of counterparties’ OpEx information and group-level Taxonomy reporting.

ESMA publishes latest edition of its newsletter 
  
  29 October 2026 
 

       
               ESMA newsletter 
           
  
              The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has published today the  latest edition of its  Spotlight on Markets newsletter  , covering key activities and publications from September and October 2026.

items.summary:
EU seeks nominations for stakeholder group on tokenisation standards in finance 
  
  09 November 2026 
 

       
               Digital Finance and Innovation 
           
  
              The European Central Bank (ECB), together with the European Commission and the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), is calling upon wholesale financial industry stakeholders to express their interest in joining the European Tokenisation Standards Group (ETSG). The group will bring together industry stakeholders to develop common standards for an interconnected tokenised financial ecosystem. 
 
      
              The group aims to establish a framework for monitoring compliance with the agreed standards and may formulate recommendations for EU authorities on how to incentivise compliance with those standards. items.title: DRSP supervisory responsibilities remain unchanged following ESMA assessment
items.summary:
DRSP supervisory responsibilities remain unchanged following ESMA assessment 
  
  18 November 2026 
 

       
               Market data 
               Supervision 
           
  
              The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has finalised its annual assessment of the derogation criteria for  Data Reporting Services Providers (DRSPs) . 
 
      
               ESMA’s supervisory responsibilities for DRSPs will remain unchanged, as the ten DRSPs currently supervised by ESMA continue to exceed the relevant derogation thresholds, while the derogated DRSPs remain under the supervision of their respective national competent authorities (NCAs). The assessment is based on data from the 2025 calendar year.  
   Next steps   
  Following the notification of the outcome of the assessment, ESMA will continue to monitor developments and engage with NCAs and supervised entities to ensure a smooth and transparent supervisory process.

items.summary: How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders. items.title: Man sentenced over £154m fake takeover bid targeting UK-listed company
items.summary:
Christopher Woolcott has today been given a 2-year prison sentence, suspended for 2 years, after staging a £154m fake takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration Inc.

He was also ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and to pay costs of £4,627.73.Mr Woolcott built a sizeable stake in Touchstone, an oil and gas listed company. He then launched a bogus bid to drive up its share price. To give the bid credibility, Mr Woolcott invented several identities, forged takeover documents using Chat GPT and met Touchstone’s chief executive at a central London hotel under a false name. Touchstone ultimately determined that the bid was not legitimate.Had his plan succeeded, he stood to gain as much as £70,000 through the sale of his shares.The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) used a combination of its transaction reporting data, phone records, receipts, CCTV footage and evidence seized to identify Mr Woolcott as the person behind the fraud.Investigators traced three phone numbers used by different supposed individuals to contact Touchstone, to the same handset, and combined voter-register, open source research and FCA trading data to narrow down potential suspects. items.title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
items.summary:
Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected.

The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. items.title: Helping more people break the cycle of persistent credit card debt
items.summary: Credit cards are a useful financial tool for many – offering flexibility and helping people manage spending and cash flow.But if customers only make low repayments over a long period, they can end up in debt for years while racking up interest and charges.The persistent debt rules we introduced in 2018 aimed to tackle this.They said that lenders had to identify customers who, over an 18-month period, paid more in interest, fees and charges than towards their balance.Lenders had to contact these customers and encourage them to increase repayments if they could afford it, and if they were still struggling, lenders had to take additional steps to help them repay their balances sustainably.What changed for consumersOur evaluation shows that consumer outcomes improved between 2018 and early 2023. items.title: Geordie Shore star and illegal finfluencer sentenced for promoting high-risk investments on social media
items.summary:
Aaron Chalmers, a reality TV star and social media content creator, and finfluencer Jason Agbodza have been sentenced for illegally promoting an unauthorised foreign exchange trading scheme on social media.

Chalmers, 39 and from Newcastle, was sentenced at City of London Magistrates Court. He previously pleaded guilty and today (19 November) was fined £3,072 and ordered to pay costs of £2,836.Having risen to fame on Geordie Shore, Chalmers has more than 2 million followers on Instagram. Agbodza, 35, of London, was also fined £1,173 and ordered to pay costs of £2,114 after pleading guilty.Both men encouraged followers to invest in foreign exchange (forex or FX) trading through contracts for difference (CFDs), without being authorised to promote them. CFDs are high-risk derivatives, and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has previously found that approximately 80% of customers lose money when investing in them.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said:'With more than two million Instagram followers, Chalmers exploited his online influence to illegally promote investments to a vast audience. items.title: Smarter regulation means understanding the trade-offs
items.summary: Regulation inevitably involves choices.Protecting consumers and maintaining confidence in our markets are fundamental to what we do. But rules also have costs. They can affect businesses’ decisions to invest, innovate and compete. Good regulation means recognising those trade-offs and using evidence to decide where intervention will make the biggest difference.That is why economics matters so much to good regulation.At our annual Economics Conference, economists, academics, regulators and industry experts came together to explore how smarter financial regulation can support sustainable growth and innovation.
